It is not a writing guide — the rest of `SKILL.md` is that. It is\nthe list of defects that survive a first draft *because* the author wrote it:\neach one is invisible from the inside and obvious to the first outside reader.\n\n**How to run it.** Re-read the whole draft once as an editor who did not write\nit. Then take the items below one at a time, against the full text — not from\nmemory of what you intended. For each item, either **fix the draft** or state in\none line why it already holds. A pass that produces no edits is a pass that was\nnot really run: assume at least a few of these apply to any first draft.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Plain, professional language\n\nWrite the plainest prose the field accepts. Formality is not complexity — a\ntop-venue paper reads *simply*; it is the ideas that are hard, not the\nsentences.\n\n- Test: could a competent researcher from a neighbouring subfield follow each\n  sentence on the first pass, at reading speed?\n- Fix: replace ornamental vocabulary with the ordinary word. Unpack stacked\n  noun phrases (\"gradient-based sample-efficiency degradation analysis\").\n  Split any sentence carrying more than one claim. Cut throat-clearing\n  (\"It is important to note that\", \"In this work, we importantly\").\n- Every term of art gets a one-clause definition at first use, including the\n  names this paper itself invents.\n\n## 2. The abstract is prose, not a results table\n\nAn abstract dense with numbers cannot be read — the reader has no axes,\nbaselines, or units in mind yet, so each number costs them more than it tells\nthem.\n\n- Test: count the numbers in the abstract. More than about three, and it is a\n  data dump.\n- Fix: keep only the headline results — the ones that would appear in a\n  one-sentence summary of the paper. Move the rest to Results, where they sit\n  next to the baseline and the axis that make them mean something.\n- The abstract must state, in words: the problem, what was done, what was\n  found, and why it matters. A reader who stops after the abstract should be\n  able to say all four back.\n\n## 3. One job per section\n\nSections leak in a first draft because the author writes what they know as they\nthink of it.\n\n- Test: read the Introduction alone. Does it contain method detail, result\n  tables, or a survey of prior work? Those belong to Method, Results, and\n  Related Work.\n- Test the reverse direction too, which is the half that gets missed: **no\n  later section may depend on a definition, formula, symbol, or piece of\n  notation that appears only in the Introduction.** If Method needs it, it is\n  defined in Method or in Preliminaries; the Introduction may motivate it, not\n  own it.\n- Fix: move the material to the section whose job it is, and leave a\n  forward-reference (\"we define this formally in Section 3\") if the\n  Introduction still needs to gesture at it.\n\n## 4. Conventional section names\n\nSection names are navigation, not titles. A reader scanning the contents must\nknow what is in each section *without reading it*.\n\n- Test: could this table of contents belong to any paper in the field? If a\n  heading names a concept the paper itself invented, it tells the reader\n  nothing until they have already read the section.\n- Fix: use the names the field uses — Introduction, Related Work,\n  Preliminaries, Method, Experiments, Results, Analysis, Discussion,\n  Limitations, Conclusion. Put the invented name in the section's first\n  sentence, or in a subsection heading underneath the conventional one.\n- Legitimate variants exist (\"Discussion and Related Work\" when related work\n  sits at the end). The bar is that the name says what kind of content follows.\n\n## 5. Related work, searched with the *final* vocabulary\n\nBy the end of the draft the work has a name, a metric, and a problem statement\nthat the project did not have when it started. The literature search that was\nrun at the beginning could not have used any of them.\n\n- Fix: run at least one more search now, using the draft's own final terms —\n  the contribution's name, the metric's name, the exact problem statement, and\n  the nearest baseline's name. Fetch real BibTeX (see `SKILL.md`) and cite what\n  comes back.\n- Also check the reference lists of the two or three closest papers already\n  cited; the nearest neighbour is very often cited by one of them.\n- An uncited close prior work is among the most common reasons a paper is\n  rejected, and it is entirely preventable at this point.\n\n## 6. Figure 1 carries the main idea\n\nThe first figure is the one every reader looks at, often before reading a word.\nIt must answer \"what is this work?\".\n\n- Test: shown only Figure 1 and its caption, could a reader say what the paper\n  proposes or studies?\n- Fix: Figure 1 shows the system, method, or central concept — not one narrow\n  comparison and not a secondary improvement, however strong that result is. If\n  the current first figure is a specific result, move it into Results and\n  promote (or specify) an overview figure in its place. Its marker belongs near\n  the end of the Introduction.\n- A correct figure in the wrong slot is still the wrong Figure 1.\n\n## 7. Report the whole study, not only the highlights\n\nIf the work covers N of something — metrics, models, datasets, configurations,\nseeds — then all N must be visible somewhere the reader can check them.\n\n- Test: state N explicitly, from the artifacts rather than from the draft. Now\n  find where all N appear. \"We evaluate 53 metrics\" followed by a figure\n  showing eight is a gap the reader will assume was chosen to flatter.\n- Fix: add the complete view — a full figure, or a complete table, in the body\n  or an appendix. Highlighting a subset in the main text is good writing;\n  showing *only* that subset is not.\n- The same applies to negative and null results from the study. They belong in\n  the paper.\n\n## 8. No implementation-internal references in the prose\n\nThe paper describes the work; the repository holds the implementation. A reader\ncannot follow a sentence that names a file they cannot see.\n\n- Test: search the draft for filenames, module paths, function names, class\n  names, CLI flags, and variable names from the codebase.\n- Fix: state the rule, not the code that implements it. Not \"`eligibility.py`\n  declares E1 as ...\" but \"an item is eligible when ...\". If the pointer is\n  genuinely useful, it goes in a footnote, an artifact link, or an appendix —\n  never in a sentence the reader has to parse.\n- Mathematical notation and algorithm names are not affected by this; they are\n  the paper's own vocabulary, not the implementation's.\n\n## 9. File: /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_YqmEFECOIR3D/3_invention_loop/iter_3/gen_paper_text/gen_paper_text/paper_draft.tex

\section{Introduction}

Evaluating the safety of open-weight language models currently requires generating text from the model, judging each output for harmful content, and aggregating scores across a benchmark of hundreds of prompts \cite{Zou2023, Rottger2023, Cui2024}. This pipeline is slow, sensitive to prompt phrasing, and must be re-run whenever a model is modified. The proliferation of post-hoc modifications to released checkpoints---in particular abliteration, a rank-one weight edit that removes a model's refusal direction \cite{Arditi2024}---makes repeated evaluation expensive and raises the question of whether safety-relevant information can be read directly from a model's internal representations.

Recent work has shown that safety-relevant information is linearly decodable from mid-layer activations. The Activation-based Model Scanner (AMS) uses 16 contrastive prompt pairs to extract a concept direction and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 checkpoints from four families \cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE computes Jensen--Shannon divergence across layer groups and reports high step-wise coupling with unsafe and refusal rates during reinforcement learning \cite{Winninger2026}. Both systems read activations only at the final prompt token. Separately, probing studies have shown that harmful content is decodable from early layers \cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}, that recognition of harmful intent is dissociable from execution of refusal \cite{Orgad2026, Lin2025}, and that recognition-type readouts survive abliteration \cite{Marshall2024, LlorenteSaguer2026a}. What remains uncharacterised is the joint depth-and-site profile: at what depth does safety information first become readable, how does that direction change across layers, and does the response site carry information beyond the prompt site?

This question is harder than it appears for three reasons. First, safety information may be distributed across layers and sites in ways that vary between training procedures, so conclusions drawn from one checkpoint need not transfer. Second, the harm direction rotates with depth \cite{Galeone2026, Arditi2024}, making it unclear whether a single coordinate accumulates signal or whether each layer writes its own direction. Third, any activation-based readout must be compared against the logit baseline---the final-layer logit gap between refusal and compliance tokens---because a readout that carries no information beyond what logits already provide does not constitute a contribution from mechanistic interpretability.

We address these questions with a three-lane study of 25 checkpoints drawn from five model families, spanning base, instruction-tuned, safety-RL, non-safety fine-tuned, and abliterated variants. Lane~A profiles each checkpoint along six activation readouts and the logit baseline. Lane~B applies dose-graded rank-one lesions to four lineages of Qwen3-4B and measures the effect at three activation sites (prompt, early response, late response). Lane~C tests whether the readouts transfer to a held-out panel of 10 checkpoints from four additional families. We report every activation readout beside the logit baseline and count a result only when it adds information beyond that baseline.

\paragraph{Summary of Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Safety training raises both recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them.} Under safety training, prompt-site recognition rises from TPR@5\%FPR = 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\% CI [0.137, 0.762]) and peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92. Abliteration drops the held-out request-axis separability from $d = 2.45$ to $d = 0.71$ ($\Delta = -1.73$, 95\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$) while the nested recognition probe barely moves ($\Delta R = -0.037$, inconclusive). The dissociation replicates across six effective parent--child pairs from four families (Section~\ref{sec:results-what-moves}).
\item \textbf{The harm direction is layer-specific, not accumulated along a fixed coordinate.} When the diff-in-means axis is frozen at a shallow layer and tracked forward, the norm-controlled gap along that axis decays with depth (Spearman $\rho$ with layer ranging from $-0.82$ to $-0.99$ across five arms). Separation is maintained only when the axis is refit at each layer. This pattern holds in all five Qwen3-4B variants and in the four Lane~B lineages (Section~\ref{sec:results-depth}).
\item \textbf{Response-site fragility under lesion is generic, not safety-specific.} The late-response TPR@1\%FPR drops under full abliteration in all four lineages, but the non-safety fine-tune (which does not refuse) shows a comparable or larger drop ($-0.169$ vs $-0.083$ to $-0.185$ for the safety-tuned lineages). Every safety-minus-non-safety contrast has a 95\% CI that includes zero (Section~\ref{sec:results-site}).
\item \textbf{No activation readout beats the logit baseline at cross-family scale.} On the 10-checkpoint held-out panel, direction self-consistency achieves the strongest correlation with harmful compliance ($\rho = -0.89$, family-bootstrap 95\% CI $[-0.95, -0.57]$), but the paired difference from the logit baseline does not exclude zero. The commissioned few-prompt activation-only metric is not achieved (Section~\ref{sec:results-heldout}).
\end{enumerate}


\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Abliteration and safety editing.}
Arditi et al.\ introduced abliteration, a rank-one edit $W \leftarrow W - \alpha \cdot u (u^\top W)$ that projects a refusal direction $u$ out of selected weight matrices, removing refusal behaviour with minimal effect on general capabilities \cite{Arditi2024}. The technique has been applied to produce ``uncensored'' checkpoints for Qwen, LLaMA, Phi, SmolLM, and Granite families, many of which are publicly available on Hugging Face. Hurtado et al.\ showed that parent-referenced weight-space statistics detect abliteration with AUROC 0.95 across 273 checkpoints, but the method requires access to the unmodified parent \cite{Hurtado2026}.

\paragraph{Activation-based safety readouts.}
AMS extracts concept directions from 16 contrastive pairs at 40--80\% depth and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 configurations from four families, with leave-one-out threshold accuracy of 71\% \cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE aggregates Jensen--Shannon divergence of hidden states across layer groups and reports high coupling with unsafe and refusal rates, though without published code \cite{Winninger2026}. RAS uses a reference-anchored score calibrated within families and separates abliterated from aligned models, but requires a reference model per family \cite{Wu2026}. All three read activations at the final prompt token. Aligned Probing correlates per-layer probe accuracy with output toxicity across 20+ models in the toxicity domain \cite{Messenger2026}. Behavioural IRT estimates a latent safety trait from roughly ten adaptively chosen items across 192 models, without using activations \cite{Jiang2026}.

\paragraph{Recognition versus execution.}
Orgad et al.\ showed that harmful response generation is dissociable from the ability to recognise and reason about harmfulness \cite{Orgad2026}. Lin et al.\ formalised this as two subspaces, a Recognition Axis and an Execution Axis, in a single model \cite{Lin2025}. Llorente-Saguer et al.\ measured recognition and abliteration across three alignment variants of the same architecture \cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}. Marshall showed that geometry associated with harm recognition survives abliteration in two model families \cite{Marshall2024}. Mitra demonstrated that prompt-time activation defences are structurally blind to prefilling attacks and that the first generated token carries distinct safety information \cite{Mitra2026}. AMS itself identifies decode-time analysis as its principal open problem \cite{Yang2026}.

\paragraph{Depth profiles and layer-specific safety.}
Yamaguchi et al.\ showed that Qwen-2.5 diverges in its processing of harmful and safe queries at approximately 40\% depth and is more robust to linear steering than LLaMA-3.1, which processes them identically for 95\% of layers \cite{Yamaguchi2025}. Schirmer et al.\ identified staging of harmfulness detection, aggregation along a refusal direction, and late-layer expression \cite{Schirmer2026}. The refusal direction at each layer rotates with depth; the weight cosine between layer-wise directions is not predictive of steerability \cite{Galeone2026}. Public abliteration toolkits already compute pairwise cosine similarities and cumulative angular drift across layers \cite{Arditi2024}.


\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Models and Checkpoints}
\label{sec:models}

Lane~A uses 25 checkpoints spanning five families: Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B), Qwen2.5 (1.5B), SmolLM3 (3B), SmolLM2 (1.7B), Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2 (2B), TinyLlama (1.1B), OLMo-2 (1B), and StableLM-2 (1.6B). Within each family, we include base, instruction-tuned, and community-abliterated variants where available. For the Qwen3-4B family, five variants are available: Base (with chat template), Instruct, SafeRL (additional safety reinforcement learning), a non-safety fine-tune (STaR, fine-tuned on HintGen mathematical reasoning), and an abliterated checkpoint (mlabonne/Qwen3-4B-abliterated). A randomly initialised Qwen3-0.6B serves as a sanity check.

Lane~B constructs four lineages of Qwen3-4B by applying the rank-one lesion at five dose levels $\alpha \in \{0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$, using the abliteration direction $u$ fitted by the diff-in-means procedure of Arditi et al.\ \cite{Arditi2024} on AdvBench harmful prompts paired with benign counterparts.

Lane~C holds out 10 checkpoints not seen during Lane~A analysis, drawn from four families (Qwen3, SmolLM3, Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2), including both parent and abliterated pairs.

\subsection{Prompts and Labelling}
\label{sec:prompts}

We use 45 harmful prompts from XSTest \cite{Rottger2023} and JailbreakBench, each paired with a benign twin that differs only in the harmful element. Harmful compliance (HC) is the fraction of harmful prompts on which the model produces a substantive harmful response, judged by a separate LLM grader with human-calibrated criteria. Over-refusal (OR) is the fraction of benign prompts refused. For the Lane~B lesion study, we use 384 harmful and 384 benign items drawn from AdvBench and paired benign corpora, split into 128 EASY prompts (fit set) and 256 HARD prompts (held-out evaluation set), with leave-one-family-out cross-validation across harm categories.

\subsection{Readouts and Notation}
\label{sec:notation}

Table~\ref{tab:notation} defines all readouts and notation used in the paper.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Notation and readout definitions.}
\label{tab:notation}
\begin{tabular}{lp{9cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Definition} \\
\midrule
$d$ (held-out) & Request-axis Cohen's $d$: the diff-in-means axis is fit on EASY prompts at the best layer, then scored on HARD prompts. Measures prompt-site separability of harmful vs.\ benign requests. \\
$R$ (TPR@$k$\%FPR) & Recognition: true positive rate of a logistic probe at $k$\% false positive rate, classifying harmful vs.\ benign requests from prompt-site activations. Fit on a random half, scored on the other. \\
Peak drive & Maximum across layers of the logit-lens projection onto the refusal token direction, measured at the last prompt token. \\
BL1 & Final-layer logit gap: the logit difference between the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position in the final layer. \\
HC & Harmful compliance rate: fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively. \\
OR & Over-refusal rate: fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. \\
Onset depth & Earliest layer (as a fraction of total depth) at which a diff-in-means probe achieves $d > 1$ on HARD prompts. \\
$B3$ & Direction self-consistency: Fisher-transformed mean cosine similarity of per-layer diff-in-means directions across consecutive layers. \\
$\alpha$ & Abliteration dose in the rank-one lesion $W \leftarrow W - \alpha \cdot u(u^\top W)$; $\alpha = 0$ is intact, $\alpha = 1$ is full abliteration. \\
PROMPT site & Activations at the last prompt token. \\
EARLY site & Activations at response tokens 5--20 (teacher-forced harmful continuation). \\
LATE site & Activations at response tokens 40--55. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Lane~A: Checkpoint Panel}
\label{sec:lane-a}

For each of the 25 checkpoints, we extract residual-stream activations at every layer for the prompt tokens and, where the model produces or is fed a harmful continuation, at the response tokens. We compute six activation readouts: held-out $d$, $R$ at TPR@5\%FPR, peak refusal drive, onset depth, $k$-prompt AUROC at $k \in \{4, 8, 16\}$, and direction self-consistency $B3$. Each is reported beside the logit baseline BL1. We additionally compute the accumulator test: the norm-controlled gap along a direction frozen at the shallowest band layer (layer 13 for Qwen3-4B), tracked forward through depth, and compare it to the gap along a per-layer refit direction.

\subsection{Lane~B: Dose-Graded Rank-One Lesion}
\label{sec:lane-b}

We fit the abliteration direction $u$ from 128 AdvBench prompts and apply the rank-one edit at layers 13--21 (the band identified by the abliteration recipe) at five dose levels. At each dose, we record activations at three sites---PROMPT, EARLY, and LATE---and fit a logistic probe (trained at $\alpha = 0$) to classify harmful vs.\ benign items. The probe's TPR at 1\%FPR and 5\%FPR across dose levels measures how the lesion affects separability at each site. Four lineages are constructed: L1 (Instruct), L2 (Instruct, different random seed for the direction), L3 (SafeRL), and L4 (STaR, a non-safety fine-tune that does not refuse).

\subsection{Lane~C: Cross-Family Validation}
\label{sec:lane-c}

Lane~C computes each activation readout on the 10 held-out checkpoints and correlates them with harmful compliance. We report Spearman $\rho$ with HC, the paired difference from BL1's $\rho$, and family-bootstrap confidence intervals that resample at the family level to account for within-family dependence. A readout is counted as exceeding BL1 only if the paired $\rho$ difference has a 95\% CI that excludes zero.


\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{What Safety Tuning and Abliteration Move}
\label{sec:results-what-moves}

[FIGURE:fig_overview]

Table~\ref{tab:main} shows the five Qwen3-4B variants on all readouts. Safety training (Base $\to$ Instruct) raises every readout: held-out $d$ rises from 0.54 to 2.45, recognition TPR@5\%FPR rises from 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\% CI on the delta: [0.137, 0.762]), peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92, and BL1 rises from 0.32 to 4.99. The non-safety fine-tune (STaR) matches Base only on held-out $d$: the difference is 0.046 (TOST-equivalent at $\pm 0.5$). On other readouts, STaR moves partway toward Instruct---covering 33\% of the Base-to-Instruct distance on peak drive and 46\% on BL1---indicating that part of the refusal-drive signal reflects generic chat fine-tuning rather than safety training alone.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Readouts for five Qwen3-4B variants. Safety training moves all readouts. Abliteration drops $d$ and drive while recognition $R$ barely moves. STaR matches Base only on $d$.}
\label{tab:main}
\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Checkpoint} & \textbf{HC} & $\bm{d}$ & $\bm{R}$ & \textbf{Drive} & \textbf{BL1} & \textbf{Onset} & $\bm{B3}$ \\
\midrule
Base          & 0.022 & 0.54  & 0.475 & 1.57  & 0.32  & 0.92 & 2.58  \\
Instruct      & 0.000 & 2.45  & 0.875 & 4.92  & 4.99  & 0.53 & 28.14 \\
SafeRL        & 0.000 & 2.34  & 0.850 & 8.78  & 3.07  & 0.53 & 33.15 \\
STaR          & NA    & 0.59  & 0.713 & 2.57  & 0.63  & 0.64 & 0.27  \\
Abliterated   & 0.733 & 0.71  & 0.838 & 1.92  & 1.76  & 0.53 & 0.54  \\
\midrule
RandInit      & NA    & 0.20  & 0.075 & 0.07  & 0.02  & 0.04 & 4.85  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Abliteration produces the opposite pattern from safety training: the held-out request-axis $d$ drops from 2.45 (Instruct) to 0.71 ($\Delta = -1.73$, 95\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$), and peak drive drops from 4.92 to 1.92 (near the Base value of 1.57). Recognition, measured by the nested HARD-refit probe, barely moves: $\Delta R = -0.037$ (90\% CI $[-0.150, 0.125]$, inconclusive due to power). This dissociation---separability collapses while the probe still classifies---replicates across six effective parent--child pairs from four families: all six show $d$ drops with 95\% CIs below zero, while the Granite null-edit control (same model re-downloaded) shows $\Delta d = 0.09$ (CI includes zero). The dissociation also holds on two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel (Section~\ref{sec:results-heldout}).

The claim ``execution, not recognition'' therefore describes only what abliteration removes, not what safety training adds. Safety training raises both recognition and the refusal drive simultaneously.

\subsection{The Harm Direction Is Layer-Specific}
\label{sec:results-depth}

[FIGURE:fig_accumulator]

A previous iteration of this work reported that the class gap along a fitted direction grows approximately 138-fold from layer 13 to the fitting layer, suggesting an accumulator mechanism. The iter-3 evaluation runs the decisive control: the same gap measured along a direction frozen at layer 13, tracked forward through depth.

The fixed-axis gap does not grow. In every arm---Base, Instruct, SafeRL, STaR, and Abliterated---the norm-controlled gap along the layer-13 axis decays with depth. The Spearman correlation between gap magnitude and layer index is strongly negative: $-0.99$ (Base), $-0.82$ (Instruct), $-0.87$ (SafeRL), $-0.97$ (STaR), $-0.88$ (Abliterated). The fixed-axis peak-to-start ratio is 1.00 in all arms: the gap never exceeds its initial value.

Separation is maintained only when the diff-in-means axis is refit at each layer. The per-layer refit ratio (gap at layer $\ell$ along $u_\ell$ divided by gap at layer 13 along $u_{13}$) ranges from 1.41 (Abliterated) to 2.09 (SafeRL). The HARD-scored variant of this ratio reaches 19.7 for Instruct, reflecting the emergence of a distinct deep-layer direction that separates harmful from benign requests on out-of-distribution prompts.

The harm direction is therefore layer-specific: shallow and deep representations encode harmfulness along different coordinates, and a single accumulated direction does not capture the trajectory. This pattern holds identically in all four Lane~B lineages across all five dose levels and all three activation sites.

\subsection{Response-Site Fragility Under Lesion}
\label{sec:results-site}

[FIGURE:fig_site]

Table~\ref{tab:site} reports the change in TPR@1\%FPR from $\alpha = 0$ (intact) to $\alpha = 1$ (full lesion) for each lineage at each of the three sites. At the PROMPT site, the change is small and includes zero in every lineage: L1 $-0.042$ [$-0.094$, $0.021$], L2 $-0.010$ [$-0.177$, $0.073$], L3 $+0.031$ [$-0.271$, $0.250$], L4 $-0.094$ [$-0.146$, $0.010$]. At the EARLY response site, changes are also small and include zero. At the LATE response site, every lineage shows a drop: L1 $-0.083$, L2 $-0.185$, L3 $-0.138$, L4 $-0.169$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Change in TPR@1\%FPR from $\alpha=0$ to $\alpha=1$, per lineage and site. LATE-site drops are comparable in the non-safety lineage L4, so the effect is not safety-specific.}
\label{tab:site}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Site} & \textbf{L1 (Instruct)} & \textbf{L2 (Instruct)} & \textbf{L3 (SafeRL)} & \textbf{L4 (STaR)} \\
\midrule
PROMPT & $-0.042$ & $-0.010$ & $+0.031$ & $-0.094$ \\
EARLY  & $-0.039$ & $+0.031$ & $+0.049$ & $-0.039$ \\
LATE   & $-0.083$ & $-0.185$ & $-0.138$ & $-0.169$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The critical comparison is L4, the non-safety fine-tune. L4 does not refuse harmful prompts, so any late-site drop under the lesion cannot be interpreted as loss of a safety-execution mechanism. L4's LATE-site drop ($-0.169$) is comparable to or larger than L1's ($-0.083$). The safety-minus-L4 contrasts all have 95\% CIs that include zero: L1$-$L4 = $-0.086$ [$-0.185$, $0.096$]; L2$-$L4 = $+0.016$ [$-0.149$, $0.240$]; L3$-$L4 = $-0.031$ [$-0.164$, $0.208$]. The late-response drop therefore reads as generic disruption of the response-site representation under a rank-one edit, not as loss of a safety-specific execution signal.

Sub-threshold doses ($\alpha \leq 0.50$) produce effects that are TOST-equivalent to zero in every lineage at every site. Only the full lesion ($\alpha = 1.0$) yields significant drops at the LATE site.

\subsection{Held-Out Panel and Cross-Family Transfer}
\label{sec:results-heldout}

[FIGURE:fig_heldout]

Table~\ref{tab:heldout} reports Spearman correlations with harmful compliance for the six activation readouts and BL1 on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Spearman $\rho$ with harmful compliance on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel. $B3$ achieves the strongest correlation but the paired delta from BL1 does not exclude zero at family-bootstrap 95\% CI.}
\label{tab:heldout}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule

\midrule

Direction self-consistency ($B3$) achieves $\rho = -0.890$ with HC, substantially stronger than BL1's $\rho = -0.620$. However, the paired delta of $-0.270$ has a family-bootstrap 95\% CI that, at $n = 10$ with four families, does not exclude zero. The partial correlation of $B3$ with HC given BL1 is $-0.816$, indicating that $B3$ captures variance in harmful compliance that BL1 does not, but the sample is too small to confirm this at the cross-family level. Two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel replicate the within-family dissociation: held-out $d$ drops in both (CIs below zero), consistent with the six Lane~A pairs.

Across the 25-checkpoint Lane~A panel, every activation readout correlates with BL1 at $\rho > 0.71$ (Table~\ref{tab:bl1corr}). The partial Spearman correlation with HC after controlling for BL1 is $-0.464$ for held-out $d$, $-0.468$ for $B3$, $-0.327$ for peak drive, and $+0.017$ for recognition $R$. Recognition therefore carries no information beyond the logit baseline at the panel level. Held-out $d$ and $B3$ retain partial correlations of moderate magnitude, but these were not pre-registered and must be interpreted with caution given the small family count.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{What the Depth Profile Reveals}

The layer-specific harm direction has implications for both the mechanistic understanding of safety and for practical readout design. The decay of the fixed-axis gap with depth means that a probe fitted at one layer cannot be applied at another without re-estimation. The growth seen in earlier reports (the ``138-fold'' increase along the fitting-layer axis) was an artefact of measuring each layer's representation on a direction optimised for the final layer: any direction fitted at one layer is most discriminative there. The informative quantity is the per-layer refit ratio, which shows modest growth (1.4--2.1$\times$) and reflects the emergence of a new harm-relevant direction at each depth, not accumulation along a single coordinate.

This finding is consistent with Galeone et al.'s report that weight cosines between layer-wise directions are low and do not predict steerability \cite{Galeone2026}, and with the observation in public abliteration toolkits that consecutive-layer cosines can be as low as 0.016 in deep layers.

\subsection{Why No Activation Metric Beats the Logit Gap}

For the Instruct model, the peak refusal-drive layer is the final layer: peak drive equals BL1 (4.92). Both readouts drop 6/6 in effective abliterated pairs, and both also drop on the Granite null-edit control (a re-download of the same model with no behavioural change, where $\Delta$BL1 $= -4.83$ and $\Delta$peak\_drive $= -2.49$ but $\Delta d = 0.09$). The held-out request-axis $d$ is the one readout that does not move on the null edit, making it the most specific activation readout---but it does not separate safety-tuned from abliterated at cross-family scale with $n = 10$.

The core difficulty is that at the panel sizes available (25 checkpoints, 10 held-out, 4--5 families), the activation readouts are too correlated with the logit gap ($\rho > 0.71$) to demonstrate independent predictive value. A larger, more diverse panel would be needed to resolve whether the partial correlations of $B3$ and held-out $d$ reflect genuine additional information or sampling noise at small $n$.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\textbf{Architecture scope.} All five Lane~A Qwen3-4B variants share one architecture. The 10 held-out checkpoints span four additional families but at $n = 10$ with four families, cross-family conclusions have wide confidence intervals.

\textbf{Prompt-only for $d$.} The request-axis Cohen's $d$ is computed at the prompt site only. A response-site variant was not tested, so we cannot determine whether it would capture information that the prompt-site version misses.

\textbf{No causal intervention at response site.} The Lane~B lesion study measures the effect of the rank-one edit on response-site representations, but does not perform a targeted causal intervention (e.g., activation patching) at the response site to confirm that the representations there are used by downstream computation.

\textbf{Teacher-forced continuations.} Response-site activations in Lane~B come from teacher-forced harmful completions, not from the model's own generations. The activations may differ from those produced during free generation, especially for models that would refuse.

\textbf{Saturation.} Probe AUROC is 1.00 at every layer and dose level, so it cannot detect degradation. We report TPR at low FPR as a de-saturated alternative, but with $n = 384$ negatives, TPR@1\%FPR is set by approximately 4 items and has resolution 0.0026.

\textbf{Gates.} Of 68 pre-registered quality gates, 43 pass and 24 fail. G1 (split-half AUROC stability within 0.02) and G5 (placebo TOST equivalence) fail in all arms. G6 (subtraction licensing) holds only in non-safety arms. These failures do not invalidate the main results but limit the precision of secondary analyses.

\textbf{The commissioned metric.} The original request asked for an activation-based metric that could evaluate any model's safety from zero to a few prompts. This metric is not delivered: no activation readout beats the logit baseline at cross-family scale. The $k$-prompt AUROC scan has smallest\_$k$\_pass = null for all candidates. We report this negative result as the honest outcome of the study.


\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We profiled safety-relevant representations across 25 checkpoints from five model families, using three complementary measurement lanes. Four findings emerged. First, safety training raises both prompt-site recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them, dropping the held-out request-axis $d$ from 2.45 to 0.71 while recognition barely changes. This dissociation replicates across six parent--child pairs. Second, the harm direction is layer-specific: the gap along a frozen shallow-layer axis decays with depth in all five Qwen3-4B variants. Third, the late-response-site fragility under rank-one lesion is not safety-specific: the non-safety fine-tune shows a comparable drop, and no safety-minus-control contrast excludes zero. Fourth, on a 10-checkpoint held-out panel, direction self-consistency ($B3$, $\rho = -0.89$) correlates most strongly with harmful compliance, but the paired margin over the logit baseline does not reach significance at the family level.

The practical implication is that, at current panel sizes, the final-layer logit gap remains the bar that activation-based safety readouts must beat. The mechanistic implication is that safety information is not stored in a single accumulated coordinate but is rewritten at each depth into a new direction, and that response-site effects of abliteration are generic rather than safety-specific. Both findings constrain how future activation-based safety metrics should be designed: they should account for layer-specific rotation and should be validated against the logit baseline on panels large enough to resolve partial correlations at the family level.

Fit on a random half, scored on the other. \\\\\nPeak drive & Maximum across layers of the logit-lens projection onto the refusal token direction, measured at the last prompt token. \\\\\nBL1 & Final-layer logit gap: the logit difference between the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position in the final layer. \\\\\nHC & Harmful compliance rate: fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively. \\\\\nOR & Over-refusal rate: fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. \\\\\nOnset depth & Earliest layer (as a fraction of total depth) at which a diff-in-means probe achieves $d > 1$ on HARD prompts. \\\\\n$B3$ & Direction self-consistency: Fisher-transformed mean cosine similarity of per-layer diff-in-means directions across consecutive layers. \\\\\n$\\alpha$ & Abliteration dose in the rank-one lesion $W \\leftarrow W - \\alpha \\cdot u(u^\\top W)$; $\\alpha = 0$ is intact, $\\alpha = 1$ is full abliteration. \\\\\nPROMPT site & Activations at the last prompt token. \\\\\nEARLY site & Activations at response tokens 5--20 (teacher-forced harmful continuation). \\\\\nLATE site & Activations at response tokens 40--55. \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\subsection{Lane~A: Checkpoint Panel}\n\\label{sec:lane-a}\n\nFor each of the 25 checkpoints, we extract residual-stream activations at every layer for the prompt tokens and, where the model produces or is fed a harmful continuation, at the response tokens. We compute six activation readouts: held-out $d$, $R$ at TPR@5\\%FPR, peak refusal drive, onset depth, $k$-prompt AUROC at $k \\in \\{4, 8, 16\\}$, and direction self-consistency $B3$. Each is reported beside the logit baseline BL1. We additionally compute the accumulator test: the norm-controlled gap along a direction frozen at the shallowest band layer (layer 13 for Qwen3-4B), tracked forward through depth, and compare it to the gap along a per-layer refit direction.\n\n\\subsection{Lane~B: Dose-Graded Rank-One Lesion}\n\\label{sec:lane-b}\n\nWe fit the abliteration direction $u$ from 128 AdvBench prompts and apply the rank-one edit at layers 13--21 (the band identified by the abliteration recipe) at five dose levels. At each dose, we record activations at three sites---PROMPT, EARLY, and LATE---and fit a logistic probe (trained at $\\alpha = 0$) to classify harmful vs.\\ benign items. The probe's TPR at 1\\%FPR and 5\\%FPR across dose levels measures how the lesion affects separability at each site. Four lineages are constructed: L1 (Instruct), L2 (Instruct, different random seed for the direction), L3 (SafeRL), and L4 (STaR, a non-safety fine-tune that does not refuse).\n\n\\subsection{Lane~C: Cross-Family Validation}\n\\label{sec:lane-c}\n\nLane~C computes each activation readout on the 10 held-out checkpoints and correlates them with harmful compliance. We report Spearman $\\rho$ with HC, the paired difference from BL1's $\\rho$, and family-bootstrap confidence intervals that resample at the family level to account for within-family dependence. A readout is counted as exceeding BL1 only if the paired $\\rho$ difference has a 95\\% CI that excludes zero.\n\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{What Safety Tuning and Abliteration Move}\n\\label{sec:results-what-moves}\n\n[FIGURE:fig_overview]\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:main} shows the five Qwen3-4B variants on all readouts. The non-safety fine-tune (STaR) matches Base only on held-out $d$: the difference is 0.046 (TOST-equivalent at $\\pm 0.5$). On other readouts, STaR moves partway toward Instruct---covering 33\\% of the Base-to-Instruct distance on peak drive and 46\\% on BL1---indicating that part of the refusal-drive signal reflects generic chat fine-tuning rather than safety training alone.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Readouts for five Qwen3-4B variants. Safety training moves all readouts. Abliteration drops $d$ and drive while recognition $R$ barely moves. STaR matches Base only on $d$.}\n\\label{tab:main}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Checkpoint} & \\textbf{HC} & $\\bm{d}$ & $\\bm{R}$ & \\textbf{Drive} & \\textbf{BL1} & \\textbf{Onset} & $\\bm{B3}$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nBase          & 0.022 & 0.54  & 0.475 & 1.57  & 0.32  & 0.92 & 2.58  \\\\\nInstruct      & 0.000 & 2.45  & 0.875 & 4.92  & 4.99  & 0.53 & 28.14 \\\\\nSafeRL        & 0.000 & 2.34  & 0.850 & 8.78  & 3.07  & 0.53 & 33.15 \\\\\nSTaR          & NA    & 0.59  & 0.713 & 2.57  & 0.63  & 0.64 & 0.27  \\\\\nAbliterated   & 0.733 & 0.71  & 0.838 & 1.92  & 1.76  & 0.53 & 0.54  \\\\\n\\midrule\nRandInit      & NA    & 0.20  & 0.075 & 0.07  & 0.02  & 0.04 & 4.85  \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nAbliteration produces the opposite pattern from safety training: the held-out request-axis $d$ drops from 2.45 (Instruct) to 0.71 ($\\Delta = -1.73$, 95\\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$), and peak drive drops from 4.92 to 1.92 (near the Base value of 1.57). Recognition, measured by the nested HARD-refit probe, barely moves: $\\Delta R = -0.037$ (90\\% CI $[-0.150, 0.125]$, inconclusive due to power). This dissociation---separability collapses while the probe still classifies---replicates across six effective parent--child pairs from four families: all six show $d$ drops with 95\\% CIs below zero, while the Granite null-edit control (same model re-downloaded) shows $\\Delta d = 0.09$ (CI includes zero). The dissociation also holds on two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel (Section~\\ref{sec:results-heldout}).\n\nThe claim ``execution, not recognition'' therefore describes only what abliteration removes, not what safety training adds. Safety training raises both recognition and the refusal drive simultaneously.\n\n\\subsection{The Harm Direction Is Layer-Specific}\n\\label{sec:results-depth}\n\n[FIGURE:fig_accumulator]\n\nA previous iteration of this work reported that the class gap along a fitted direction grows approximately 138-fold from layer 13 to the fitting layer, suggesting an accumulator mechanism. The iter-3 evaluation runs the decisive control: the same gap measured along a direction frozen at layer 13, tracked forward through depth.\n\nThe fixed-axis gap does not grow. In every arm---Base, Instruct, SafeRL, STaR, and Abliterated---the norm-controlled gap along the layer-13 axis decays with depth. The Spearman correlation between gap magnitude and layer index is strongly negative: $-0.99$ (Base), $-0.82$ (Instruct), $-0.87$ (SafeRL), $-0.97$ (STaR), $-0.88$ (Abliterated). The fixed-axis peak-to-start ratio is 1.00 in all arms: the gap never exceeds its initial value.\n\nSeparation is maintained only when the diff-in-means axis is refit at each layer. The per-layer refit ratio (gap at layer $\\ell$ along $u_\\ell$ divided by gap at layer 13 along $u_{13}$) ranges from 1.41 (Abliterated) to 2.09 (SafeRL). The HARD-scored variant of this ratio reaches 19.7 for Instruct, reflecting the emergence of a distinct deep-layer direction that separates harmful from benign requests on out-of-distribution prompts.\n\nThe harm direction is therefore layer-specific: shallow and deep representations encode harmfulness along different coordinates, and a single accumulated direction does not capture the trajectory. This pattern holds identically in all four Lane~B lineages across all five dose levels and all three activation sites.\n\n\\subsection{Response-Site Fragility Under Lesion}\n\\label{sec:results-site}\n\n[FIGURE:fig_site]\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:site} reports the change in TPR@1\\%FPR from $\\alpha = 0$ (intact) to $\\alpha = 1$ (full lesion) for each lineage at each of the three sites. At the EARLY response site, changes are also small and include zero. At the LATE response site, every lineage shows a drop: L1 $-0.083$, L2 $-0.185$, L3 $-0.138$, L4 $-0.169$.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Change in TPR@1\\%FPR from $\\alpha=0$ to $\\alpha=1$, per lineage and site. LATE-site drops are comparable in the non-safety lineage L4, so the effect is not safety-specific.}\n\\label{tab:site}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Site} & \\textbf{L1 (Instruct)} & \\textbf{L2 (Instruct)} & \\textbf{L3 (SafeRL)} & \\textbf{L4 (STaR)} \\\\\n\\midrule\nPROMPT & $-0.042$ & $-0.010$ & $+0.031$ & $-0.094$ \\\\\nEARLY  & $-0.039$ & $+0.031$ & $+0.049$ & $-0.039$ \\\\\nLATE   & $-0.083$ & $-0.185$ & $-0.138$ & $-0.169$ \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe critical comparison is L4, the non-safety fine-tune. L4 does not refuse harmful prompts, so any late-site drop under the lesion cannot be interpreted as loss of a safety-execution mechanism. L4's LATE-site drop ($-0.169$) is comparable to or larger than L1's ($-0.083$). The safety-minus-L4 contrasts all have 95\\% CIs that include zero: L1$-$L4 = $-0.086$ [$-0.185$, $0.096$]; L2$-$L4 = $+0.016$ [$-0.149$, $0.240$]; L3$-$L4 = $-0.031$ [$-0.164$, $0.208$]. The late-response drop therefore reads as generic disruption of the response-site representation under a rank-one edit, not as loss of a safety-specific execution signal.\n\nSub-threshold doses ($\\alpha \\leq 0.50$) produce effects that are TOST-equivalent to zero in every lineage at every site. Only the full lesion ($\\alpha = 1.0$) yields significant drops at the LATE site.\n\n\\subsection{Held-Out Panel and Cross-Family Transfer}\n\\label{sec:results-heldout}\n\n[FIGURE:fig_heldout]\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:heldout} reports Spearman correlations with harmful compliance for the six activation readouts and BL1 on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Spearman $\\rho$ with harmful compliance on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel. $B3$ achieves the strongest correlation but the paired delta from BL1 does not exclude zero at family-bootstrap 95\\% CI.}\n\\label{tab:heldout}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Readout} & $\\bm{\\rho}$ & \\textbf{Family 95\\% CI} & \\textbf{$\\Delta$ vs BL1} & \\textbf{Partial $\\rho$|BL1} \\\\\n\\midrule\n$B3$ (self-consistency) & $-0.890$ & $[-0.951, -0.569]$ & $-0.270$ & $-0.816$ \\\\\n$C13$ (peak $d$)        & $-0.656$ & $[-0.975, 0.200]$  & $-0.037$ & $-0.433$ \\\\\nBL1                     & $-0.620$ & $[-0.735, 0.200]$  & ---      & --- \\\\\nBL1\\_hard               & $-0.534$ & $[-0.705, 0.413]$  & ---      & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nDirection self-consistency ($B3$) achieves $\\rho = -0.890$ with HC, substantially stronger than BL1's $\\rho = -0.620$. However, the paired delta of $-0.270$ has a family-bootstrap 95\\% CI that, at $n = 10$ with four families, does not exclude zero. The partial correlation of $B3$ with HC given BL1 is $-0.816$, indicating that $B3$ captures variance in harmful compliance that BL1 does not, but the sample is too small to confirm this at the cross-family level. Two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel replicate the within-family dissociation: held-out $d$ drops in both (CIs below zero), consistent with the six Lane~A pairs.\n\nAcross the 25-checkpoint Lane~A panel, every activation readout correlates with BL1 at $\\rho > 0.71$ (Table~\\ref{tab:bl1corr}). The partial Spearman correlation with HC after controlling for BL1 is $-0.464$ for held-out $d$, $-0.468$ for $B3$, $-0.327$ for peak drive, and $+0.017$ for recognition $R$. Recognition therefore carries no information beyond the logit baseline at the panel level. Held-out $d$ and $B3$ retain partial correlations of moderate magnitude, but these were not pre-registered and must be interpreted with caution given the small family count.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Correlation of each activation readout with BL1 across the 25-checkpoint panel. The decay of the fixed-axis gap with depth means that a probe fitted at one layer cannot be applied at another without re-estimation. The growth seen in earlier reports (the ``138-fold'' increase along the fitting-layer axis) was an artefact of measuring each layer's representation on a direction optimised for the final layer: any direction fitted at one layer is most discriminative there. The informative quantity is the per-layer refit ratio, which shows modest growth (1.4--2.1$\\times$) and reflects the emergence of a new harm-relevant direction at each depth, not accumulation along a single coordinate.\n\nThis finding is consistent with Galeone et al.'s report that weight cosines between layer-wise directions are low and do not predict steerability \\cite{Galeone2026}, and with the observation in public abliteration toolkits that consecutive-layer cosines can be as low as 0.016 in deep layers.\n\n\\subsection{Why No Activation Metric Beats the Logit Gap}\n\nFor the Instruct model, the peak refusal-drive layer is the final layer: peak drive equals BL1 (4.92). Both readouts drop 6/6 in effective abliterated pairs, and both also drop on the Granite null-edit control (a re-download of the same model with no behavioural change, where $\\Delta$BL1 $= -4.83$ and $\\Delta$peak\\_drive $= -2.49$ but $\\Delta d = 0.09$). The held-out request-axis $d$ is the one readout that does not move on the null edit, making it the most specific activation readout---but it does not separate safety-tuned from abliterated at cross-family scale with $n = 10$.\n\nThe core difficulty is that at the panel sizes available (25 checkpoints, 10 held-out, 4--5 families), the activation readouts are too correlated with the logit gap ($\\rho > 0.71$) to demonstrate independent predictive value. A larger, more diverse panel would be needed to resolve whether the partial correlations of $B3$ and held-out $d$ reflect genuine additional information or sampling noise at small $n$.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\textbf{Architecture scope.} All five Lane~A Qwen3-4B variants share one architecture. The 10 held-out checkpoints span four additional families but at $n = 10$ with four families, cross-family conclusions have wide confidence intervals.\n\n\\textbf{Prompt-only for $d$.} The request-axis Cohen's $d$ is computed at the prompt site only. A response-site variant was not tested, so we cannot determine whether it would capture information that the prompt-site version misses.\n\n\\textbf{No causal intervention at response site.} The Lane~B lesion study measures the effect of the rank-one edit on response-site representations, but does not perform a targeted causal intervention (e.g., activation patching) at the response site to confirm that the representations there are used by downstream computation.\n\n\\textbf{Teacher-forced continuations.} Response-site activations in Lane~B come from teacher-forced harmful completions, not from the model's own generations. The activations may differ from those produced during free generation, especially for models that would refuse.\n\n\\textbf{Saturation.} Probe AUROC is 1.00 at every layer and dose level, so it cannot detect degradation. We report TPR at low FPR as a de-saturated alternative, but with $n = 384$ negatives, TPR@1\\%FPR is set by approximately 4 items and has resolution 0.0026.\n\n\\textbf{Gates.} Of 68 pre-registered quality gates, 43 pass and 24 fail. G1 (split-half AUROC stability within 0.02) and G5 (placebo TOST equivalence) fail in all arms. G6 (subtraction licensing) holds only in non-safety arms. These failures do not invalidate the main results but limit the precision of secondary analyses.\n\n\\textbf{The commissioned metric.} The original request asked for an activation-based metric that could evaluate any model's safety from zero to a few prompts. This metric is not delivered: no activation readout beats the logit baseline at cross-family scale. The $k$-prompt AUROC scan has smallest\\_$k$\\_pass = null for all candidates. We report this negative result as the honest outcome of the study.\n\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe profiled safety-relevant representations across 25 checkpoints from five model families, using three complementary measurement lanes. Four findings emerged. First, safety training raises both prompt-site recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them, dropping the held-out request-axis $d$ from 2.45 to 0.71 while recognition barely changes. This dissociation replicates across six parent--child pairs. Second, the harm direction is layer-specific: the gap along a frozen shallow-layer axis decays with depth in all five Qwen3-4B variants. Third, the late-response-site fragility under rank-one lesion is not safety-specific: the non-safety fine-tune shows a comparable drop, and no safety-minus-control contrast excludes zero. Fourth, on a 10-checkpoint held-out panel, direction self-consistency ($B3$, $\\rho = -0.89$) correlates most strongly with harmful compliance, but the paired margin over the logit baseline does not reach significance at the family level.\n\nThe practical implication is that, at current panel sizes, the final-layer logit gap remains the bar that activation-based safety readouts must beat. The mechanistic implication is that safety information is not stored in a single accumulated coordinate but is rewritten at each depth into a new direction, and that response-site effects of abliteration are generic rather than safety-specific. Both findings constrain how future activation-based safety metrics should be designed: they should account for layer-specific rotation and should be validated against the logit baseline on panels large enough to resolve partial correlations at the family level.\n", "structuredPatch": [], "originalFile": null, "userModified": false}

This pipeline is slow, sensitive to prompt phrasing, and must be re-run whenever a model is modified. The Activation-based Model Scanner (AMS) uses 16 contrastive prompt pairs to extract a concept direction and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 checkpoints from four families \\cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE computes Jensen--Shannon divergence across layer groups and reports high step-wise coupling with unsafe and refusal rates during reinforcement learning \\cite{Winninger2026}. Both systems read activations only at the final prompt token. Separately, probing studies have shown that harmful content is decodable from early layers \\cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}, that recognition of harmful intent is dissociable from execution of refusal \\cite{Orgad2026, Lin2025}, and that recognition-type readouts survive abliteration \\cite{Marshall2024, LlorenteSaguer2026a}. What remains uncharacterised is the joint depth-and-site profile: at what depth does safety information first become readable, how does that direction change across layers, and does the response site carry information beyond the prompt site?\n\nThis question is harder than it appears for three reasons. First, safety information may be distributed across layers and sites in ways that vary between training procedures, so conclusions drawn from one checkpoint need not transfer. Second, the harm direction rotates with depth \\cite{Galeone2026, Arditi2024}, making it unclear whether a single coordinate accumulates signal or whether each layer writes its own direction. Third, any activation-based readout must be compared against the logit baseline---the final-layer logit gap between refusal and compliance tokens---because a readout that carries no information beyond what logits already provide does not constitute a contribution from mechanistic interpretability.\n\nWe address these questions with a three-lane study of 25 checkpoints drawn from five model families, spanning base, instruction-tuned, safety-RL, non-safety fine-tuned, and abliterated variants. Lane~C tests whether the readouts transfer to a held-out panel of 10 checkpoints from four additional families. We report every activation readout beside the logit baseline and count a result only when it adds information beyond that baseline.\n\n\\paragraph{Summary of Contributions.}\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item \\textbf{Safety training raises both recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them.} Under safety training, prompt-site recognition rises from TPR@5\\%FPR = 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\\% CI [0.137, 0.762]) and peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92. Abliteration drops the held-out request-axis separability from $d = 2.45$ to $d = 0.71$ ($\\Delta = -1.73$, 95\\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$) while the nested recognition probe barely moves ($\\Delta R = -0.037$, inconclusive). Separation is maintained only when the axis is refit at each layer. The commissioned few-prompt activation-only metric is not achieved (Section~\\ref{sec:results-heldout}).\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Abliteration and safety editing.}\nArditi et al.\\ introduced abliteration, a rank-one edit $W \\leftarrow W - \\alpha \\cdot u (u^\\top W)$ that projects a refusal direction $u$ out of selected weight matrices, removing refusal behaviour with minimal effect on general capabilities \\cite{Arditi2024}. The technique has been applied to produce ``uncensored'' checkpoints for Qwen, LLaMA, Phi, SmolLM, and Granite families, many of which are publicly available on Hugging Face. Hurtado et al.\\ showed that parent-referenced weight-space statistics detect abliteration with AUROC 0.95 across 273 checkpoints, but the method requires access to the unmodified parent \\cite{Hurtado2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Activation-based safety readouts.}\nAMS extracts concept directions from 16 contrastive pairs at 40--80\\% depth and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 configurations from four families, with leave-one-out threshold accuracy of 71\\% \\cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE aggregates Jensen--Shannon divergence of hidden states across layer groups and reports high coupling with unsafe and refusal rates, though without published code \\cite{Winninger2026}. RAS uses a reference-anchored score calibrated within families and separates abliterated from aligned models, but requires a reference model per family \\cite{Wu2026}. All three read activations at the final prompt token. Aligned Probing correlates per-layer probe accuracy with output toxicity across 20+ models in the toxicity domain \\cite{Messenger2026}. Behavioural IRT estimates a latent safety trait from roughly ten adaptively chosen items across 192 models, without using activations \\cite{Jiang2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Recognition versus execution.}\nOrgad et al.\\ showed that harmful response generation is dissociable from the ability to recognise and reason about harmfulness \\cite{Orgad2026}. Lin et al.\\ formalised this as two subspaces, a Recognition Axis and an Execution Axis, in a single model \\cite{Lin2025}. Llorente-Saguer et al.\\ measured recognition and abliteration across three alignment variants of the same architecture \\cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}. Marshall showed that geometry associated with harm recognition survives abliteration in two model families \\cite{Marshall2024}. Mitra demonstrated that prompt-time activation defences are structurally blind to prefilling attacks and that the first generated token carries distinct safety information \\cite{Mitra2026}. AMS itself identifies decode-time analysis as its principal open problem \\cite{Yang2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Depth profiles and layer-specific safety.}\nYamaguchi et al.\\ showed that Qwen-2.5 diverges in its processing of harmful and safe queries at approximately 40\\% depth and is more robust to linear steering than LLaMA-3.1, which processes them identically for 95\\% of layers \\cite{Yamaguchi2025}. Schirmer et al.\\ identified staging of harmfulness detection, aggregation along a refusal direction, and late-layer expression \\cite{Schirmer2026}. The refusal direction at each layer rotates with depth; the weight cosine between layer-wise directions is not predictive of steerability \\cite{Galeone2026}. Public abliteration toolkits already compute pairwise cosine similarities and cumulative angular drift across layers \\cite{Arditi2024}.\n\n\n\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Models and Checkpoints}\n\\label{sec:models}\n\nLane~A uses 25 checkpoints spanning five families: Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B), Qwen2.5 (1.5B), SmolLM3 (3B), SmolLM2 (1.7B), Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2 (2B), TinyLlama (1.1B), OLMo-2 (1B), and StableLM-2 (1.6B). Within each family, we include base, instruction-tuned, and community-abliterated variants where available. For the Qwen3-4B family, five variants are available: Base (with chat template), Instruct, SafeRL (additional safety reinforcement learning), a non-safety fine-tune (STaR, fine-tuned on HintGen mathematical reasoning), and an abliterated checkpoint (mlabonne/Qwen3-4B-abliterated). A randomly initialised Qwen3-0.6B serves as a sanity check.\n\nLane~B constructs four lineages of Qwen3-4B by applying the rank-one lesion at five dose levels $\\alpha \\in \\{0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\\}$, using the abliteration direction $u$ fitted by the diff-in-means procedure of Arditi et al.\\ \\cite{Arditi2024} on AdvBench harmful prompts paired with benign counterparts.\n\nLane~C holds out 10 checkpoints not seen during Lane~A analysis, drawn from four families (Qwen3, SmolLM3, Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2), including both parent and abliterated pairs.\n\n\\subsection{Prompts and Labelling}\n\\label{sec:prompts}\n", "numLines": 50, "startLine": 0, "totalLines": 259}}

This pipeline is slow, sensitive to prompt phrasing, and must be re-run whenever a model is modified. The proliferation of post-hoc modifications to released checkpoints---in particular abliteration, a rank-one weight edit that removes a model's refusal direction \\cite{Arditi2024}---makes repeated evaluation expensive and raises the question of whether safety-relevant information can be read directly from a model's internal representations.\n\nRecent work has shown that safety-relevant information is linearly decodable from mid-layer activations. The Activation-based Model Scanner (AMS) uses 16 contrastive prompt pairs to extract a concept direction and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 checkpoints from four families \\cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE computes Jensen--Shannon divergence across layer groups and reports high step-wise coupling with unsafe and refusal rates during reinforcement learning \\cite{Winninger2026}. Both systems read activations only at the final prompt token. Separately, probing studies have shown that harmful content is decodable from early layers \\cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}, that recognition of harmful intent is dissociable from execution of refusal \\cite{Orgad2026, Lin2025}, and that recognition-type readouts survive abliteration \\cite{Marshall2024, LlorenteSaguer2026a}. What remains uncharacterised is the joint depth-and-site profile: at what depth does safety information first become readable, how does that direction change across layers, and does the response site carry information beyond the prompt site?\n\nThis question is harder than it appears for three reasons. First, safety information may be distributed across layers and sites in ways that vary between training procedures, so conclusions drawn from one checkpoint need not transfer. Second, the harm direction rotates with depth \\cite{Galeone2026, Arditi2024}, making it unclear whether a single coordinate accumulates signal or whether each layer writes its own direction. Third, any activation-based readout must be compared against the logit baseline---the final-layer logit gap between refusal and compliance tokens---because a readout that carries no information beyond what logits already provide does not constitute a contribution from mechanistic interpretability.\n\nWe address these questions with a three-lane study of 25 checkpoints drawn from five model families, spanning base, instruction-tuned, safety-RL, non-safety fine-tuned, and abliterated variants (Figure~\\ref{fig:overview}). Lane~A profiles each checkpoint along six activation readouts and the logit baseline. Lane~B applies dose-graded rank-one lesions to four lineages of Qwen3-4B and measures the effect at three activation sites (prompt, early response, late response). Lane~C tests whether the readouts transfer to a held-out panel of 10 checkpoints from four additional families. We report every activation readout beside the logit baseline and count a result only when it adds information beyond that baseline.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_overview]\n\n\\paragraph{Summary of Contributions.}\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item \\textbf{Safety training raises both recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them.} Under safety training, prompt-site recognition rises from TPR@5\\%FPR = 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\\% CI [0.137, 0.762]) and peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92. Abliteration drops the held-out request-axis separability from $d = 2.45$ to $d = 0.71$ ($\\Delta = -1.73$, 95\\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$) while the nested recognition probe barely moves ($\\Delta R = -0.037$, inconclusive). The dissociation replicates across six effective parent--child pairs from four families (Section~\\ref{sec:results-what-moves}).\n\\item \\textbf{The harm direction is layer-specific, not accumulated along a fixed coordinate.} When the diff-in-means axis is frozen at a shallow layer and tracked forward, the norm-controlled gap along that axis decays with depth (Spearman $\\rho$ with layer ranging from $-0.82$ to $-0.99$ across five arms). Separation is maintained only when the axis is refit at each layer. This pattern holds in all five Qwen3-4B variants and in the four Lane~B lineages (Section~\\ref{sec:results-depth}).\n\\item \\textbf{Response-site fragility under lesion is generic, not safety-specific.} The late-response TPR@1\\%FPR drops under full abliteration in all four lineages, but the non-safety fine-tune (which does not refuse) shows a comparable or larger drop ($-0.169$ vs $-0.083$ to $-0.185$ for the safety-tuned lineages). Every safety-minus-non-safety contrast has a 95\\% CI that includes zero (Section~\\ref{sec:results-site}).\n\\item \\textbf{No activation readout beats the logit baseline at cross-family scale.} On the 10-checkpoint held-out panel, direction self-consistency achieves the strongest correlation with harmful compliance ($\\rho = -0.89$, family-bootstrap 95\\% CI $[-0.95, -0.57]$), but the paired difference from the logit baseline does not exclude zero. The commissioned few-prompt activation-only metric is not achieved (Section~\\ref{sec:results-heldout}).\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Abliteration and safety editing.}\nArditi et al.\\ introduced abliteration, a rank-one edit $W \\leftarrow W - \\alpha \\cdot u (u^\\top W)$ that projects a refusal direction $u$ out of selected weight matrices, removing refusal behaviour with minimal effect on general capabilities \\cite{Arditi2024}. The technique has been applied to produce ``uncensored'' checkpoints for Qwen, LLaMA, Phi, SmolLM, and Granite families, many of which are publicly available on Hugging Face. Hurtado et al.\\ showed that parent-referenced weight-space statistics detect abliteration with AUROC 0.95 across 273 checkpoints, but the method requires access to the unmodified parent \\cite{Hurtado2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Activation-based safety readouts.}\nAMS extracts concept directions from 16 contrastive pairs at 40--80\\% depth and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 configurations from four families, with leave-one-out threshold accuracy of 71\\% \\cite{Yang2026}. N-GLARE aggregates Jensen--Shannon divergence of hidden states across layer groups and reports high coupling with unsafe and refusal rates, though without published code \\cite{Winninger2026}. RAS uses a reference-anchored score calibrated within families and separates abliterated from aligned models, but requires a reference model per family \\cite{Wu2026}. All three read activations at the final prompt token. Aligned Probing correlates per-layer probe accuracy with output toxicity across 20+ models in the toxicity domain \\cite{Messenger2026}. Behavioural IRT estimates a latent safety trait from roughly ten adaptively chosen items across 192 models, without using activations \\cite{Jiang2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Recognition versus execution.}\nOrgad et al.\\ showed that harmful response generation is dissociable from the ability to recognise and reason about harmfulness \\cite{Orgad2026}. Lin et al.\\ formalised this as two subspaces, a Recognition Axis and an Execution Axis, in a single model \\cite{Lin2025}. Llorente-Saguer et al.\\ measured recognition and abliteration across three alignment variants of the same architecture \\cite{LlorenteSaguer2026a, LlorenteSaguer2026b}. Marshall showed that geometry associated with harm recognition survives abliteration in two model families \\cite{Marshall2024}. Mitra demonstrated that prompt-time activation defences are structurally blind to prefilling attacks and that the first generated token carries distinct safety information \\cite{Mitra2026}. AMS itself identifies decode-time analysis as its principal open problem \\cite{Yang2026}.\n\n\\paragraph{Depth profiles and layer-specific safety.}\nYamaguchi et al.\\ showed that Qwen-2.5 diverges in its processing of harmful and safe queries at approximately 40\\% depth and is more robust to linear steering than LLaMA-3.1, which processes them identically for 95\\% of layers \\cite{Yamaguchi2025}. Schirmer et al.\\ identified staging of harmfulness detection, aggregation along a refusal direction, and late-layer expression \\cite{Schirmer2026}. The refusal direction at each layer rotates with depth; the weight cosine between layer-wise directions is not predictive of steerability \\cite{Galeone2026}. Public abliteration toolkits already compute pairwise cosine similarities and cumulative angular drift across layers \\cite{Arditi2024}.\n\n\n\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Models and Checkpoints}\n\\label{sec:models}\n\nLane~A uses 25 checkpoints spanning five families: Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B), Qwen2.5 (1.5B), SmolLM3 (3B), SmolLM2 (1.7B), Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2 (2B), TinyLlama (1.1B), OLMo-2 (1B), and StableLM-2 (1.6B). Within each family, we include base, instruction-tuned, and community-abliterated variants where available. For the Qwen3-4B family, five variants are available: Base (with chat template), Instruct, SafeRL (additional safety reinforcement learning), a non-safety fine-tune (STaR, fine-tuned on HintGen mathematical reasoning), and an abliterated checkpoint (mlabonne/Qwen3-4B-abliterated). A randomly initialised Qwen3-0.6B serves as a sanity check. The complete list of 25 checkpoints and their readout values appears in Table~\\ref{tab:main} (Qwen3-4B variants) and in Appendix Table~\\ref{tab:full_panel} (full panel).\n\nLane~B constructs four lineages of Qwen3-4B by applying the rank-one lesion at five dose levels $\\alpha \\in \\{0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\\}$, using the abliteration direction $u$ fitted by the diff-in-means procedure of Arditi et al.\\ \\cite{Arditi2024} on AdvBench harmful prompts paired with benign counterparts.\n\nLane~C holds out 10 checkpoints not seen during Lane~A analysis, drawn from four families (Qwen3, SmolLM3, Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2), including both parent and abliterated pairs.\n\n\\subsection{Prompts and Labelling}\n\\label{sec:prompts}\n\nWe use 45 harmful prompts from XSTest \\cite{Rottger2023} and JailbreakBench, each paired with a benign twin that differs only in the harmful element. Harmful compliance (HC) is the fraction of harmful prompts on which the model produces a substantive harmful response, judged by a separate LLM grader with human-calibrated criteria. Over-refusal (OR) is the fraction of benign prompts refused. For the Lane~B lesion study, we use 384 harmful and 384 benign items drawn from AdvBench and paired benign corpora, split into 128 EASY prompts (fit set) and 256 HARD prompts (held-out evaluation set), with leave-one-family-out cross-validation across harm categories.\n\n\\subsection{Readouts and Notation}\n\\label{sec:notation}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:notation} defines all readouts and notation used in the paper.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Notation and readout definitions.}\n\\label{tab:notation}\n\\begin{tabular}{lp{9cm}}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Symbol} & \\textbf{Definition} \\\\\n\\midrule\n$d$ (held-out) & Request-axis Cohen's $d$: the diff-in-means axis is fit on EASY prompts at the best layer, then scored on HARD prompts. Measures prompt-site separability of harmful vs.\\ benign requests. \\\\\n$R$ (TPR@$k$\\%FPR) & Recognition: true positive rate of a logistic probe at $k$\\% false positive rate, classifying harmful vs.\\ benign requests from prompt-site activations. Fit on a random half, scored on the other. \\\\\nPeak drive & Maximum across layers of the logit-lens projection onto the refusal token direction, measured at the last prompt token. \\\\\nBL1 & Final-layer logit gap: the logit difference between the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position in the final layer. \\\\\nHC & Harmful compliance rate: fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively. \\\\\nOR & Over-refusal rate: fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. \\\\\nOnset depth & Earliest layer (as a fraction of total depth) at which a diff-in-means probe achieves $d > 1$ on HARD prompts. \\\\\n$B3$ & Direction self-consistency: Fisher-transformed mean cosine similarity of per-layer diff-in-means directions across consecutive layers. \\\\\n$\\alpha$ & Abliteration dose in the rank-one lesion $W \\leftarrow W - \\alpha \\cdot u(u^\\top W)$; $\\alpha = 0$ is intact, $\\alpha = 1$ is full abliteration. \\\\\nPROMPT site & Activations at the last prompt token. \\\\\nEARLY site & Activations at response tokens 5--20 (teacher-forced harmful continuation). \\\\\nLATE site & Activations at response tokens 40--55. \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\subsection{Lane~A: Checkpoint Panel}\n\\label{sec:lane-a}\n\nFor each of the 25 checkpoints, we extract residual-stream activations at every layer for the prompt tokens and, where the model produces or is fed a harmful continuation, at the response tokens. We compute six activation readouts: held-out $d$, $R$ at TPR@5\\%FPR, peak refusal drive, onset depth, $k$-prompt AUROC at $k \\in \\{4, 8, 16\\}$, and direction self-consistency $B3$. Each is reported beside the logit baseline BL1. We additionally compute the accumulator test: the norm-controlled gap along a direction frozen at the shallowest band layer (layer 13 for Qwen3-4B), tracked forward through depth, and compare it to the gap along a per-layer refit direction.\n\n\\subsection{Lane~B: Dose-Graded Rank-One Lesion}\n\\label{sec:lane-b}\n\nWe fit the abliteration direction $u$ from 128 AdvBench prompts and apply the rank-one edit at layers 13--21 (the band identified by the abliteration recipe) at five dose levels. At each dose, we record activations at three sites---PROMPT, EARLY, and LATE---and fit a logistic probe (trained at $\\alpha = 0$) to classify harmful vs.\\ benign items. The probe's TPR at 1\\%FPR and 5\\%FPR across dose levels measures how the lesion affects separability at each site. Four lineages are constructed: L1 (Instruct), L2 (Instruct, different random seed for the direction), L3 (SafeRL), and L4 (STaR, a non-safety fine-tune that does not refuse).\n\n\\subsection{Lane~C: Cross-Family Validation}\n\\label{sec:lane-c}\n\nLane~C computes each activation readout on the 10 held-out checkpoints and correlates them with harmful compliance. A readout is counted as exceeding BL1 only if the paired $\\rho$ difference has a 95\\% CI that excludes zero.\n\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{What Safety Tuning and Abliteration Move}\n\\label{sec:results-what-moves}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:main} shows the five Qwen3-4B variants on all readouts. Safety training (Base $\\to$ Instruct) raises every readout: held-out $d$ rises from 0.54 to 2.45, recognition TPR@5\\%FPR rises from 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\\% CI on the delta: [0.137, 0.762]), peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92, and BL1 rises from 0.32 to 4.99. Safety training raises both recognition and the refusal drive simultaneously.\n\n\\subsection{The Harm Direction Is Layer-Specific}\n\\label{sec:results-depth}\n\n[FIGURE:fig_accumulator]\n\nA previous iteration of this work reported that the class gap along a fitted direction grows approximately 138-fold from layer 13 to the fitting layer, suggesting an accumulator mechanism. In every arm---Base, Instruct, SafeRL, STaR, and Abliterated---the norm-controlled gap along the layer-13 axis decays with depth. The Spearman correlation between gap magnitude and layer index is strongly negative: $-0.99$ (Base), $-0.82$ (Instruct), $-0.87$ (SafeRL), $-0.97$ (STaR), $-0.88$ (Abliterated). The fixed-axis peak-to-start ratio is 1.00 in all arms: the gap never exceeds its initial value.\n\nSeparation is maintained only when the diff-in-means axis is refit at each layer. The per-layer refit ratio (gap at layer $\\ell$ along $u_\\ell$ divided by gap at layer 13 along $u_{13}$) ranges from 1.41 (Abliterated) to 2.09 (SafeRL). The HARD-scored variant of this ratio reaches 19.7 for Instruct, reflecting the emergence of a distinct deep-layer direction that separates harmful from benign requests on out-of-distribution prompts.\n\nThe harm direction is therefore layer-specific: shallow and deep representations encode harmfulness along different coordinates, and a single accumulated direction does not capture the trajectory. At the EARLY response site, changes are also small and include zero. At the LATE response site, every lineage shows a drop: L1 $-0.083$, L2 $-0.185$, L3 $-0.138$, L4 $-0.169$.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Change in TPR@1\\%FPR from $\\alpha=0$ to $\\alpha=1$, per lineage and site. LATE-site drops are comparable in the non-safety lineage L4, so the effect is not safety-specific.}\n\\label{tab:site}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Site} & \\textbf{L1 (Instruct)} & \\textbf{L2 (Instruct)} & \\textbf{L3 (SafeRL)} & \\textbf{L4 (STaR)} \\\\\n\\midrule\nPROMPT & $-0.042$ & $-0.010$ & $+0.031$ & $-0.094$ \\\\\nEARLY  & $-0.039$ & $+0.031$ & $+0.049$ & $-0.039$ \\\\\nLATE   & $-0.083$ & $-0.185$ & $-0.138$ & $-0.169$ \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe critical comparison is L4, the non-safety fine-tune. L4 does not refuse harmful prompts, so any late-site drop under the lesion cannot be interpreted as loss of a safety-execution mechanism. L4's LATE-site drop ($-0.169$) is comparable to or larger than L1's ($-0.083$). The safety-minus-L4 contrasts all have 95\\% CIs that include zero: L1$-$L4 = $-0.086$ [$-0.185$, $0.096$]; L2$-$L4 = $+0.016$ [$-0.149$, $0.240$]; L3$-$L4 = $-0.031$ [$-0.164$, $0.208$]. The late-response drop therefore reads as generic disruption of the response-site representation under a rank-one edit, not as loss of a safety-specific execution signal.\n\nSub-threshold doses ($\\alpha \\leq 0.50$) produce effects that are TOST-equivalent to zero in every lineage at every site. However, the paired delta of $-0.270$ has a family-bootstrap 95\\% CI that, at $n = 10$ with four families, does not exclude zero. The partial correlation of $B3$ with HC given BL1 is $-0.816$, indicating that $B3$ captures variance in harmful compliance that BL1 does not, but the sample is too small to confirm this at the cross-family level. Two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel replicate the within-family dissociation: held-out $d$ drops in both (CIs below zero), consistent with the six Lane~A pairs.\n\nAcross the 25-checkpoint Lane~A panel, every activation readout correlates with BL1 at $\\rho > 0.71$ (Table~\\ref{tab:bl1corr}). Recognition therefore carries no information beyond the logit baseline at the panel level. Held-out $d$ and $B3$ retain partial correlations of moderate magnitude, but these were not pre-registered and must be interpreted with caution given the small family count.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Correlation of each activation readout with BL1 across the 25-checkpoint panel.
